title: Operating systems & filesystems
summary: Match the platform to the workload.

passages.heading: The core idea
passages.markdown: An operating system manages hardware resources and provides services to applications. Desktop platforms such as Windows, Linux, and macOS differ in supported applications, management tools, and hardware compatibility. Mobile platforms emphasize touch input, battery management, and controlled application permissions. Choosing a platform starts with the required applications, supported hardware, organizational policies, and the vendor’s supported life cycle rather than personal familiarity alone.

passages.heading: In the real world
passages.markdown: A filesystem organizes stored data and defines features such as permissions, journaling, and size limits. NTFS is common for Windows system volumes and supports access permissions. APFS is associated with modern Apple systems, and ext4 is common on Linux. exFAT can be useful for removable media shared between platforms, while FAT32 has a roughly four-gigabyte single-file limit. A device recognizing a physical disk does not guarantee that it can read every filesystem on that disk. Before formatting, preserve needed data and verify the intended systems can read the chosen format.

passages.heading: Make it stick
passages.markdown: Put it into practice by explaining the decision in your own words. In a support scenario, identify the requirement first, connect it to the relevant technology, and check the result against that requirement. If the evidence changes, revisit your reasoning rather than repeating the same action. Document what you observed so the next person can understand your conclusion.
